''capitata'' Tausch |''Berberis dulcis'' K.Koch |''Berberis dumetorum'' Gouan |''Berberis edulis'' K.Koch |''Berberis elongata'' G.Nicholson |''Berberis globularis'' G.Nicholson |''Berberis hakodate'' Dippel |''Berberis heterophylla'' K.Koch |''Berberis iberica'' Sweet |''Berberis innominata'' Kielm. |''Berberis irritabilis'' Salisb. |''Berberis jacquinii'' K.Koch |''Berberis latifolia'' Poit. & Turpin |''Berberis marginata'' K.Koch |''Berberis maxima'' G.Nicholson |''Berberis maximowiczii'' Regel |''Berberis microphylla'' F.Dietr. |''Berberis mitis'' Schrad. |''Berberis nepalensis'' K.Koch |''Berberis nitens'' Schrad. |''Berberis obovata'' Schrad. |''Berberis orientalis'' C.K.Schneid. |''Berberis pangharengensis'' G.Nicholson |''Berberis pauciflora'' Salisb. |''Berberis racemosa'' Stokes |''Berberis rubra'' Poit. & Turpin |''Berberis sanguinea'' K.Koch |''Berberis sanguinolenta'' K.Koch |''Berberis sibirica'' Schult. & Schult.f. |''Berberis sieboldii'' Dippel |''Berberis sylvestris'' Poit. & Turpin |''Berberis violacea'' Poit. & Turpin }} | synonyms_ref = [http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2674612 The Plant List] }} '''''Berberis vulgaris''''', also known as '''common barberry''',{{PLANTS|id=BEVU|taxon=Berberis vulgaris|access-date=24 March 2016}} '''European barberry''' or simply '''barberry''', is a [[shrub]] in the genus ''[[Berberis]]'' native to the [[Old World]]. It produces edible but sharply acidic berries, which people in many countries eat as a tart and refreshing fruit. ==Description== It is a [[deciduous]] shrub growing up to {{convert|4|m|abbr=off}} high. The [[leaves]] are small, oval, {{convert|2–5|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long and {{convert|1–2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} broad, with a serrated margin; they are borne in clusters of 2–5 together, subtended by a three-branched spine {{convert|3–8|mm|frac=16}} long.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}} The [[flower]]s are yellow, {{convert|4–6|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} across, produced on {{convert|3–6|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long [[panicle]]s in late spring. The [[fruit]] is an oblong red [[berry (botany)|berry]] {{convert|7–10|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long and {{convert|3–5|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} broad, ripening in late summer or autumn. Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 29.2 days, and bears an average of 1.3 seeds per fruit. Fruits average 76% water, and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 6.5% [[carbohydrate]]s and 1.2% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}} File:Berberis-vulgaris-flowers.jpg|Leaves File:歐洲小蘗 Berberis vulgaris -匈牙利布達佩斯 Budapest, Hungary- (9216101912).jpg|Flowers File:Berberis vulgaris .jpg|Fruit ==Subspecies== {{As of|2024|March}}, [[Plants of the World Online]] accepted three subspecies:{{Cite POWO|title=''Berberis vulgaris'' L..|id=328527-2|access-date=2024-03-13|mode=cs1}} *[[Berberis vulgaris subsp. australis|''Berberis vulgaris'' subsp. ''australis'']] (Boiss.) Heywood *''Berberis vulgaris'' subsp. ''seroi'' O.Bolòs & Vigo *''Berberis vulgaris'' subsp. ''vulgaris'' ==Distribution and habitat== The shrub is native to central and southern Europe, southern [[England]],[https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.8ca Plant Atlas 2020] northwest Africa and [[western Asia]];[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=berberis+vulgaris Altervista Flora Italiana, Crespino comune, Sowberry, Common Barberry, vinettier, espino cambrón, Sauerdorn, ''Berberis vulgaris'' L. ] includes photos, drawings, and European distribution map it is also [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in northern Europe and North America. In the United States and Canada, it has become established in the wild over an area from [[Nova Scotia]] to [[Nebraska]], with additional populations in [[Colorado]], [[Idaho]], [[Washington state]], [[Montana]], and [[British Columbia]].[http://www.efloras.org/object_page.aspx?object_id=5734&flora_id=1 Flora of North America vol 3] It is also cultivated in many countries. == Ecology == The berries are an important food for many small birds, which disperse the seeds in their droppings. ''B. vulgaris'' is the [[alternate host]] species of the wheat stem rust fungus ([[Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici|''Puccinia graminis'' f. sp. ''tritici'']]), a grass-infecting [[Rust (fungus)|rust fungus]] that is a serious fungal disease of [[wheat]] and related grains. For this reason, cultivation of ''B. vulgaris'' is prohibited in Canada{{cite web |date=2012-04-03 |title=D-01-04: Plant protection import and domestic movement requirements for barberry (''Berberis'', ''Mahoberberis'' and ''Mahonia'' spp.) under the Canadian Barberry Certification Program |url=http://www.inspection.gc.ca/plants/plant-protection/directives/horticulture/d-01-04/eng/1333479606359/1333480359713 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402101550/http://www.inspection.gc.ca/plants/plant-protection/directives/horticulture/d-01-04/eng/1333479606359/1333480359713 |archive-date=2015-04-02 |access-date=2015-03-07}} and some areas of the US ([[Connecticut]], [[Massachusetts]], [[Michigan]], and [[New Hampshire]]). == Phytochemistry == The main compounds are [[Isoquinoline alkaloids|isoquinoline]] and protoberberine alkaloids; the primary constituents include [[berberine]], oxyacanthine, [[palmatine]], berberrubine, lambertine, obamegine, aromoline, [[columbamine]], berlambine, tejedine, berbidine, and [[berbamine]].{{Cite journal |last=Chukwuneme |first=Chinenyenwa Fortune |last2=Gildenhuys |first2=Samantha |date=2026-02-01 |title=Systems analysis of ''Berberis vulgaris'' alkaloids unveils their functional synergy and drug-like potential |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1476927125003597 |journal=Computational Biology and Chemistry |volume=120 |article-number=108698 |pmid= 41033163 |doi=10.1016/j.compbiolchem.2025.108698 |issn=1476-9271|doi-access=free }} The fruits were found to contain the [[Terpenoid|terpenoids]] [[lupeol]] and [[oleanolic acid]], as well as the steroids [[stigmasterol]] and stigmasterol [[glucoside]].{{Cite journal |last=Saied |first=S. |last2=Begum |first2=S. |date=2004-03-01 |title=Phytochemical Studies of Berberis vulgaris |url=https://doi.org/10.1023/B:CONC.0000033929.60336.bb |journal=Chemistry of Natural Compounds |language=en |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=137–140 |doi=10.1023/B:CONC.0000033929.60336.bb |issn=1573-8388|url-access=subscription }} == Uses == [[File:Dried barberries on a plate.JPG|thumb|left|Dried barberries]] The edible berries,{{Cite book |last1=Elias |first1=Thomas S. |title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods |last2=Dykeman |first2=Peter A. |publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9 |location=New York |pages=219 |oclc=244766414 |orig-year=1982}} though rich in [[vitamin C]], have a very sharp or sour flavour and are not widely consumed because the thorny shrubs make them difficult to harvest. In Europe, the berries have been traditionally used as an ingredient in making [[jam]]. The berries are high in [[pectin]] which makes the jam congeal as it cools after having been boiled. In southwestern Asia, especially Iran, the berries are used for cooking, as well as for jam-making. In Iran, barberries are commonly used as a currant in [[rice pilaf]]. {{lang|fa|[[wikt:زرشک#Persian|زرشک]]}} ''zerešk'' is the [[Persian language|Persian]] name for the dried [[fruit]] of ''Berberis'' spp., particularly also that of ''[[Berberis integerrima]]'' called {{lang|fa|زرشک [[wikt:بی‌دانه#Persian|بی‌دانه]]}} ''zerešk bi-dâne'', literally 'seedless barberry',{{cite journal |last1=Alemardan |first1=Ali |last2=Asadi |first2=Wahab |last3=Rezaei |first3=Mehdi |last4=Tabrizi |first4=Leila |last5=Mohammadi |first5=Siavash |year=2013 |title=Cultivation of Iranian seedless barberry (''Berberis integerrima'' 'Bidaneh'): A medicinal shrub |journal=Industrial Crops and Products |volume=50 |pages=276–87 |doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2013.07.061}} which is widely cultivated in [[Iran]]. Iran is the largest producer of ''zerešk''. The [[South Khorasan]] province in [[Iran]] is the main area of ''zerešk'' and [[saffron]] production in the world, especially around [[Birjand]] and [[Qaen]]. About 85% of production is in Qaen and about 15% in Birjand. There is evidence of cultivation of seedless barberry in South Khorasan two hundred years ago.{{cite book |last1=Tehranifar |first1=A. |title=XXVI International Horticultural Congress: Asian Plants with Unique Horticultural Potential: Genetic Resources, Cultural Practices, and Utilization |year=2003 |isbn=978-90-66054-00-4 |editor1-last=Lee |editor1-first=J-M. |series=ISHS Acta Horticulturae 620 |pages=193–5 |chapter=Barberry Growing in Iran |editor2-last=Zhang |editor2-first=D. |chapter-url=http://www.actahort.org/books/620/620_21.htm |access-date=15 January 2014 |archive-date=27 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150927200358/http://www.actahort.org/books/620/620_21.htm |url-status=dead }} A garden of ''zerešk'' is called {{lang|fa|زرشکستان}} ''zerešk-[[-stan|estân]]''. Zerešk is widely used in cooking, imparting a tart flavour to chicken dishes. It is usually cooked with [[rice]], called {{lang|fa|زرشک [[wikt:پلو#Persian|پلو]]}} ''zerešk polo'', and provides a meal with chicken. === Other uses === The plant has been widely cultivated for hedges in [[New Zealand]].{{cite book |title=An Illustrated Guide to Common Weeds of New Zealand |publisher=New Zealand Plant Protection Society |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-473-16285-6 |editor1-last=Popay |editor1-first=Ian |edition=3rd |location=Christchurch |chapter=''Berberis glaucocarpa'' barberry |editor2-last=Champion |editor2-first=Paul |editor3-last=James |editor3-first=Trevor |chapter-url=http://www.rnzih.org.nz/pages/berberisglaucocarpa.htm}}{{page needed|date=January 2014}} A [[decoction]] of the plant has been used as a folk medicine to treat [[gastrointestinal]] ailments and coughs,{{cite book |last1=Schauenberg |first1=P |title=Guide to Medicinal Plants |last2=Paris |first2=F |publisher=Keats Publishing, Inc. |year=1977 |location=New Canaan, CT}} although its use has been limited due to the bitter taste of the bark and root.{{cite book |last=Duke |first=JA |title=Handbook of Medicinal Herbs |publisher=CRC Press |year=1985 |location=Boca Raton, Florida}}{{cite journal |last1=Hartwell |first1=JL |year=1971 |title=Plants used against cancer. A survey. |journal=Lloydia |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=386–425 |pmid=5173435}} ==See also== *''[[Berberis microphylla]]'', ''calafate'' (a related shrub with similar berries, native in temperate South America) ==References== {{Reflist|30em}} ==Bibliography== * {{cite journal |date=1991 |first1=Johan |last1=Ehrlén |first2=Ove |last2=Eriksson |title=Phenological variation in fruit characteristics in vertebrate-dispersed plants |pages=463–470 |doi=10.1007/BF00318311 |journal=Oecologia |issn=0029-8549 |volume=86 |issue=4}} ==External links== {{Commons}} *[http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Berberis+&SPECIES_XREF=vulgaris&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= Flora Europaea: ''Berberis vulgaris'' distribution] {{Herbs & spices}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q158563}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Berberis|vulgaris]] [[Category:Medicinal plants of Africa]] [[Category:Medicinal plants of Asia]] [[Category:Medicinal plants of Europe]] [[Category:Plants described in 1753]] [[Category:Spices]] [[Category:Botanical taxa named by Carl Linnaeus]] [[Category:Plants with thorns]]
